title: Commonly confused words
note: Many errors are the wrong word, not bad grammar. Affect is usually a verb (to influence) and effect usually a noun (a result). Lie means recline (lie, lay, lain) and takes no object; lay means put (lay, laid, laid) and takes one. Use fewer with plural things you count and less with amounts.

src.t: Writing for Success, 4.1 Commonly Confused Words, LibreTexts

items.c: The new law had a big ___. (affect/effect)
I need to ___ down for a nap. (lie/lay)
She ___ the book down an hour ago. (laid/lay)
Yesterday the cat ___ in the sun. (lay/laid)
He has ___ in bed all day. (lain/laid)
Cite, site or sight: 'to quote a source'
Emigrate or immigrate: 'to leave a country'

items.ex: 'Raise' needs an object: stores raise prices.

read.title: Hooks for near-miss words
text: Some word pairs trip up even practiced writers because they sound alike or look alike. A few memory hooks settle most of them.

For affect and effect, remember that affect is usually the action and effect the end result: "The weather affected the game; the effect was a long delay." The rarer uses, such as effect as a verb meaning to bring about, are worth learning once and then watching for.

For lie and lay, ask whether the verb has an object. Lay always does: you lay something down. Lie never does: you simply lie down. The difficulty is that the past tense of lie is lay. "Yesterday I lay on the couch" is correct; "Yesterday I laid the book on the couch" is also correct, because laid is the past tense of lay.
For fewer and less, use fewer for separate things you can count and less for a mass or amount: fewer cars, less traffic. Idioms such as "less than ten miles" treat the number as one amount.
For contractions such as it's, they're and you're, read the apostrophe aloud as the missing letters. If "it is" or "they are" fits, the contraction is right.

q.q: Why is "Yesterday I lay on the couch" correct?
o: Lay is the past tense of lie
Lay is the present tense of lie

q.q: Which phrase follows the reading's rule for fewer and less?
What test does the reading give for it's?
o: Read it as it is and see if it fits
Use it only at the start of a sentence
